claims.text: High-temperature melt-and-quench synthesis yields single-phase Al0.1CrCoFeNi solid-solution nanoparticles.
Intermediate-temperature annealing promotes atomic-scale short-range chemical order.
Rapid quenching retains a fully random solid solution in Al0.1CrCoFeNi nanoparticles.
Short-range chemical order is associated with variations in the local lattice-strain distribution.
Short-range ordering raises local atomic-diffusion activation barriers by locking atoms into favorable configurations and relieving local configurational stress.
Higher diffusion barriers suppress phase segregation.
Higher diffusion barriers slow grain-boundary migration and grain coarsening.
Randomly quenched nanoparticles have faster diffusion kinetics than short-range-ordered nanoparticles under identical high-temperature conditions.
Faster diffusion in the random state promotes clustering and phase separation.
Between 700 and 900 °C, nanoparticles with enhanced short-range order will coarsen more slowly than the rapidly quenched baseline.
Between 700 and 900 °C, nanoparticles with enhanced short-range order will exhibit less phase segregation than the rapidly quenched baseline.
Between 700 and 900 °C, nanoparticles with enhanced short-range order will maintain greater chemical homogeneity than the rapidly quenched baseline.
The stabilization effect will diminish above approximately 900 °C because thermal energy overcomes ordering-induced diffusion barriers.
Thermal instability of short-range order above the proposed range can cause the ordered and quenched states to equilibrate and reduce their contrast.
Existing simulation and experimental studies support the qualitative trend that short-range order suppresses diffusion-driven grain growth and segregation in this system.

A controlled comparison can test the hypothesis by measuring short-range order, grain-size evolution, and phase separation in annealed and rapidly quenched Al0.1CrCoFeNi nanoparticles under identical conditions.
